newsitem.title: USA: U.S. securities group says new law will cut costs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. securities group says new law will cut costs.

text.p: A trade group for U.S. brokers and investment banks reiterated on Friday its position that a new securities law overhauling state and federal regulation will lower the costs of raising capital.
The Securities Industry Association (SIA) trade group did not comment directly after President Bill Clinton signed the National Capital Markets Efficiency Act of 1996 into law.
But a spokeswoman noted the SIA issued a statement October one upon congressional passage of the bill hailing the measure as "an important bipartisan achievement for the 104th congress."

"Needless, redundant and antiquated state and federal regulations add to the cost of capital, making it more expensive for companies to raise money to expand and create jobs, while reducing returns for investors," SIA president Marc Lackritz said in a statement issued at the time.

The SIA said important features of the bill would allow broker-dealers greater flexibility to borrow funds; establish uniform standards for broker-dealer books and record-keeping; improve efficiency of regulation governing investment advisers; broaden the Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) exemptive authority to address outdated or inconsistent statutes; enable securities firms' mutual funds to produce readable prospectuses by eliminating redundant and inconsistent state regulations and promote meaningful coordination among authorities in conducting routine examinations.

Officials of securities firms have long maintained that various checks of their books by federal and state regulators and the self-regulatory organizatons such as the stock exchanges, are duplicative and add to costs.
